# REA: Reverse Engineer Anything

### One MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior.

**See a feature you like. Understand how it works, down to the binary level.**

See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project.

REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion.

Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine.

> **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies.

## Quick start

On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron
analysis require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's `PATH` for process ownership
checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/installation.md` under
"Linux owned-process prerequisite".

### Set up your agent

With Node.js and npm installed, run:

```bash
npx rea-agents setup
```

Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds
REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing
configuration. Restart your agent afterward.

Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and
[other agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents). See
[installation and setup](docs/installation.md) for provider configuration and
manual MCP registration.

MCP uses compact input schemas by default to reduce context overhead. Set
`REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full` in your MCP registration when you need the
complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles
keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See
"Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide.

### Ask your agent

```text
Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a
similar feature for my project.
```

Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand.

### Use the terminal

Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json
```

The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence.
Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows.

To install the `rea` command for regular use:

```bash
npm install --global rea-agents
rea --help
```

For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the
[CLI and Evidence guide](docs/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection,
snapshots and scripting.

### Update REA

REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your
installation up to date.

For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`:

```bash
rea update
```

`rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global
output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls.

Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized
metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue
with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure
and waits for submitted writes to finish.

Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release,
upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`.

To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed
by the update.

If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with:

```bash
npx rea-agents@latest setup
```

Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands,
use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use
`bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`.

## How REA works

Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code.
REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up
questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation.
CLI commands use the same workflows.

![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg)

[Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg).

## What you can analyze

REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm.
Additional tools and host support depend on the target:

| Target                  | What REA returns                                                                                  | Requirements and guide                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Desktop installations   | Runtime candidates, supporting files, component markers and next probes                           | Built-in bounded directory/header inspection; [desktop applications](docs/desktop-applications.md)                                    |
| Native binaries         | Pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls and references                                      | Hopper, Ghidra or IDA; [native analysis](docs/native-investigation.md)                                                                |
| Offline ELF layout      | Sections, segments, original symbols/relocations and static mitigation candidates                 | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; [binary diagnostics](docs/binary-diagnostics.md)                                               |
| Go binaries             | Embedded compiler version, modules, replacements and build settings                               | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; no Go installation required                                                            |
| GPU code objects        | CUDA/HIP targets, selected kernel parameters and resources, retained PTX text                     | Built-in static ELF/PE/fatbin/CUBIN/PTX inspection; [GPU code objects](docs/gpu-code-objects.md)                                      |
| Model artifacts         | GGUF / safetensors metadata, tensor declarations and derived totals                               | Built-in header inspection; optional full-file hash; [model files](docs/model-artifacts.md)                                           |
| IL2CPP metadata         | Unity global-metadata.dat assembly images, type and method names and index ranges                 | Built-in static decoding of versions 24, 27, 29, 31 and 39; no Unity required                                                         |
| Godot PCK               | Archive inventory and extraction, original header/directory facts and selected content identities | Built-in static formats 2, 3 and 4; no Godot required                                                                                 |
| Rust binaries           | Embedded cargo-auditable crate names, versions, sources and dependency edges                      | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; [Rust binaries](docs/rust-binaries.md)                                                 |
| PE certificates         | Authenticode WIN_CERTIFICATE entries and PKCS#7 signer/X.509 identity fields                      | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE certificates](docs/pe-certificates.md)                                                             |
| ELF notes               | PT_NOTE/SHT_NOTE owners, types, GNU build-id and ABI-tag fields                                   | Built-in static ELF inspection; [ELF notes](docs/elf-notes.md)                                                                        |
| Erlang BEAM             | IFF chunks, atoms, exports, imports, lambdas and the Code header                                  | Built-in static BEAM inspection; [Erlang BEAM](docs/erlang-beam.md)                                                                   |
| WASM artifact           | Validation, sections, exact import/export WAT forms and decoded WAT                               | Caller-supplied WABT 1.0.42; `inspect_wasm_artifact`                                                                                  |
| EVM bytecode            | Dispatch selectors, byte offsets, inferred arguments and mutability                               | Local raw/hex carrier on Linux x64; [offline EVM guide](docs/evm-bytecode.md)                                                         |
| SQLite databases        | Tables, columns, indexes, views, triggers and selected ordinary-table rows                        | Local database/WAL snapshot; Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ with native SQLite limits                                                    |
| Recorded Linux crashes  | Raw notes, every recorded thread's registers/signals and optional mapping candidates              | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; optional GDB/pwndbg; [recorded crashes](docs/recorded-crashes.md)                              |
| JavaScript / Electron   | Modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC and native add-on relationships                        | Node.js and npm; Linux: procps-compatible `ps`; [application analysis](docs/javascript-application-workflows.md)                      |
| Websites                | Page structure, scripts, network observations and requested screenshots                           | A Chrome-family browser; [browser analysis](docs/browser-observation.md)                                                              |
| Saved network captures  | Requests, responses, exposed payloads and source locations                                        | HAR or Fiddler Everywhere SAZ; mitmdump on Linux for native mitmproxy; [capture guide](docs/web-network-captures.md)                  |
| .NET assemblies         | Metadata, CIL instructions, declared native dependencies and build comparisons                    | None (static only); [managed-code guide](docs/managed-code-analysis.md)                                                               |
| Android APKs            | Manifest declarations, classes, decompiled methods and references                                 | Headless JADX and a full JDK on Linux/macOS/Windows x64; [Android guide](docs/android-analysis.md)                                    |
| APK signatures          | v1/v2/v3/v3.1 signers, certificate fingerprints, key rotation and digest self-consistency         | None (static only); `inspect_apk_signature`                                                                                           |
| Android devices         | Devices, packages, processes, logs, dumps, screen captures, and APK/file transfers                | Caller-supplied adb (emulator or hardware); [ADB guide](docs/adb-device-analysis.md)                                                  |
| JEB projects            | Engine-backed project units, artifact digests and type/method pseudo-code                         | A caller-started JEB client serving MCP, selected with REA_JEB_MCP_URL; [JEB guide](docs/jeb-analysis.md)                             |
| Android resources       | Decoded manifest, string tables, locales and version facts                                        | Caller-supplied Apktool launcher; [resource guide](docs/apktool-resource-analysis.md)                                                 |
| Flutter apps            | Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance                           | None (static APK parsing); [Flutter guide](docs/flutter-analysis.md)                                                                  |
| Firmware                | Regions, extraction results and native-analysis handoffs                                          | Binwalk / Unblob on Linux; [firmware guide](docs/firmware-analysis.md)                                                                |
| Recorded packets        | Selected fields, repeated values, filters and decode-as rules                                     | Linux: TShark 4.x + prlimit; [capture guide](docs/packet-captures.md)                                                                 |
| Packet summaries        | Endpoints, DNS, TLS SNI, protocol distribution and HTTP requests                                  | Caller-supplied tshark and capinfos (Linux-verified); [pcap guide](docs/pcap-analysis.md)                                             |
| Recorded logic signals  | Decoder annotations, sample ranges and diagnostics                                                | Linux: sigrok-cli 0.7.2 + prlimit; [signal recordings](docs/signal-recordings.md)                                                     |
| Packages and resources  | File inventories, digests, plists, Apple bundle anatomy and extracted resources                   | [Artifact and JavaScript guide](docs/javascript-artifact-reconstruction.md), [Apple applications](docs/apple-application-analysis.md) |
| Process behavior        | Terminal output, interactions, exit and filesystem observations, and run comparisons              | Linux/macOS with a native PTY; [process capture](docs/process-capture.md)                                                             |
| PyInstaller executables | CArchive members, Python version, entry scripts and extracted bytecode                            | None (static only); [Python packaged applications](docs/python-packaged-applications.md)                                              |

Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running
the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target
using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects.

For offline native-binary inspection, REA also supports caller-supplied GNU
objdump and Rizin. See the [reverse-engineering tools guide](docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md)
for provider setup, CLI commands, and Evidence limitations. REA does not install
or update either provider.

<a id="choosing-a-deep-analysis-provider"></a>

Native formats and host support vary by provider. See
[Hopper and Ghidra setup](docs/installation.md#hopper), the
[IDA guide](docs/ida-provider.md) (including an optional native MCP bridge), the
[Kuna decompiler guide](docs/kuna-provider.md), and
[experimental Windows Ghidra support](docs/windows-ghidra-p0.md).
Ghidra also supports [16-bit DOS analysis](docs/ghidra-dos.md).
For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with
`REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS` or `REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS`.
For provider selection, see the [CLI guide](docs/cli.md#choose-a-provider).
Check [release availability](docs/installation.md#released-package-and-main)
for features added since the latest npm release.

## Showcases

[![Illustrations of the DX-Ball sound-pan, Notion clipboard-bridge, and TH04 bullet-ring showcases](docs/assets/rea-showcases.png)](https://rea.tools/showcase/)

### DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation

Follow a sound call into its position-to-pan helper, inspect the instructions,
and turn incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passes 3,205
original-x86 cases and reproduces all 63 compiled function bytes.

[Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/dx-ball/) ·
[Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/dx-ball)

### Notion: trace the Electron clipboard bridge

Find the renderer's clipboard API, follow it through preload and IPC into the
main process, and inspect the rich clipboard format.

[Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/notion/)

### TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring calculation

Inspect the original PC-98 game's 16-bit instructions, recover the fixed and
aimed angle calculations, and compare the reconstructed C++ with the
historical compiler output.

[Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/th04/) ·
[Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04)

If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your
case in an [issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) or a
[pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls), including the target,
your question, how REA helped, and what you found.

## FAQ

<details>
<summary><strong>Which agents can use REA?</strong></summary>

Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the
[supported agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents); other clients can use
[manual MCP registration](docs/installation.md#mcp-registry).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Do I need Hopper, Ghidra or IDA?</strong></summary>

Deep native analysis uses one of them. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection
work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval;
Ghidra and IDA use your existing installations. See [provider setup](docs/installation.md#hopper).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Do I need to start Hopper first?</strong></summary>

REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may
ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the
same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open
Hopper manually if needed. See
[Hopper startup and troubleshooting](docs/installation.md#launcher-paths-and-troubleshooting).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>What does installing the skill from skills.sh do?</strong></summary>

The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use `npx rea-agents setup`
to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart
your agent. See [skill-only installation](docs/installation.md#skill-only-installation).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>What code does REA return?</strong></summary>

Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis
recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to
write and test an implementation; the [showcases](#showcases) give worked examples.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Does REA upload my app?</strong></summary>

REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its
model provider has its own data policy.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>What should I do if I hit a bug?</strong></summary>

Update first; a recent release may already fix it.

For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`:

```bash
rea update
```

For agent setup through `npx`:

```bash
npx rea-agents@latest setup
```

If you're using an agent, complete the [setup refresh](#update-rea) and restart
it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues)
with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.

</details>

## Documentation

Start with the website's [worked guides](https://rea.tools/guides/).
For exact options, prerequisites and result contracts:

- [Installation and setup](docs/installation.md): agent registration, provider configuration, updates and uninstall.
- [Readiness and troubleshooting](docs/installation.md#check-readiness-for-your-task): diagnose one agent or analysis engine.
- [CLI and Evidence](docs/cli.md): commands, provider selection, snapshots, import/export and exit statuses.
- [MCP contracts](docs/mcp-contracts.md) and [agent prompts](docs/mcp-prompts.md): tool results, sessions and guided investigations.
- [Tool catalog](docs/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog): generated inventory of tools, providers and CLI commands.
- [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md): planned work and capability trackers.

Report vulnerabilities through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Disclaimer

See [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md) for responsible-use guidance.

The project's position on illegal or unauthorized use covers all REA versions,
distribution channels, and platforms; each copy retains its applicable licenses.

REA is for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation,
and analysis of software you own or are authorized to examine.

## Contributing

We'd love your help with REA! [Open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) to
report a bug or suggest a feature, or [send a pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls)
to improve the code or docs.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup and checks,

<skill_content name="reverse-engineer-anything">
# Skill: reverse-engineer-anything

# REA

Use REA when a claim depends on a shipped binary or package, decompilation,
passive application runtime evidence, or comparison with
behavior not established by available source. For ordinary analysis of a
complete source repository, use normal repository tools and do not run REA
readiness or provider commands.

## Connect only when needed

Installing this skill supplies instructions; it does not register the REA MCP
server, install analysis engines, or add tools to an already-running agent.

If REA tools are available and their registration is not known to be stale,
proceed directly to the target. Do not run diagnostics or setup before every
investigation. Use the connected server's actual tool list and input schemas;
a skill installed from repository main may describe capabilities absent from
an older npm release. Keep complete inline Evidence when that server does not
advertise retained references.

If tools are absent, a call is blocked by the client, or a required provider is
unavailable, read [connection and recovery](references/connection-and-recovery.md).
Diagnose the observed blocker, continue useful supported work, and resume the
original task after repair. Client approval, shell PATH, registration and engine
availability have different remedies; avoid repeating setup for all of them.

1. Diagnose without changing REA or client configuration. `npx` may download
   the package and write to npm's cache. For Codex, run
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 doctor --client codex --json`. Substitute the current
   supported client: `claude_code`, `claude_desktop`, `codex`, `cursor`,
   `gemini_cli`, `windsurf`, `devin`, `opencode`, `antigravity`, `copilot_cli`,
   `commandcode`, `vscode`, `grok_build`, `omp`, or `grok_bot`. `grok_bot` has no local
   file registration: doctor reports the Grok Bot chat step, and setup does not
   write `mcp.json`. If the client is unknown, use `doctor --json` and
   inspect its registration results before choosing a setup scope.
2. Distinguish the reason. Missing, malformed, or stale registration needs a
   scoped configuration repair. An aligned registration with no tools in the
   active session needs a restart/reconnection; doctor cannot prove that the
   current agent has connected. A missing provider affects only tasks requiring
   that provider: static JavaScript inspection needs neither Hopper nor Ghidra,
   and Android inspection has separate bring-your-own JADX/Java prerequisites.
3. For a configuration repair, prepare the read-only plan:
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 setup --client codex --dry-run --json`.
   Use the current client's ID, show its exact proposed paths, backups, and
   changes, and obtain approval before setup writes configuration or installs
   Hopper. Setup normally installs the matching bundled skill too; include that
   replacement in the reviewed plan. After approval, apply the same scope with
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 setup --client codex --yes`. Add `--install-hopper`
   only if that separate installation was needed and explicitly approved.
4. Restart/reconnect the affected agent. Verify that REA tools actually appear
   in the session, then resume the original investigation. If they remain
   absent, inspect the client's MCP launch error rather than repeating setup.

REA setup never installs or upgrades Node.js, npm, Homebrew, Java, Ghidra, IDA,
JADX, Kuna, Binwalk, or Unblob. Use existing prerequisites; do not install unrelated
software to repair
MCP registration. For an unsupported client, use manual stdio registration
with a version-pinned `rea-agents` package or continue through the CLI.

A concrete CLI fallback for an operator-supplied JavaScript tree or ASAR is:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json
```

No MCP registration or native engine is required. Read the returned Evidence,
graph, limitations, and unknowns with the same care as an MCP result; the CLI
returns the Evidence record directly. This fallback does not establish that
MCP is configured. Native CLI tasks still require their selected engine.
Prefer an existing `rea` CLI. When none is installed and REA package acquisition
is within the authorized scope, use `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0` in its place.
Configuration repair starts with a read-only setup plan; show paths, backups and
skill replacement before applying authorized changes. Preserve existing approval
and target-execution boundaries. REA setup never installs or upgrades unrelated
software, including Node.js, npm, Homebrew, Java, Ghidra, IDA, JADX, Kuna, Binwalk or Unblob.

## Route the target first

Choose the first tool from the target the user supplied. Use `open_binary` for
active-target native or archive workflows; target-free tools take their own
explicit path or endpoint and do not need it.

- ASAR or extracted JavaScript/Electron tree:
  `analyze_javascript_application`.
- Archive/package member inventory (ZIP/APK/IPA/MSIX/AppX or DMG):
  `open_binary` with the supplied local path; use `inspect_artifact` when its
  graph and findings help answer the question.
- Android APK code, classes, methods, or incoming references:
  `inspect_android_package`, then focused Android tools when advertised.
  Archive member inventory still uses the archive route above.
- Managed PE/CLI assembly: `inspect_managed_artifact`.
- Firmware image: `inspect_firmware_regions` when advertised. Use
  `extract_firmware` when extraction is requested, with a caller-selected new
  absolute output directory. These tools use caller-supplied Binwalk/Unblob on
  Linux; see the [firmware guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/firmware-analysis.md).
- .NET NativeAOT PE/ELF: native Ghidra analysis. Native code can yield pseudocode;
  consult the NativeAOT workflow in `references/native-and-artifacts.md` for
  optional metadata recovery and its supported host/layout boundary.
- User-owned browser page already open: `list_browser_targets`.
- Browser action the agent must perform (click, type, navigate):
  `capture_browser_scenario` with declared actions. See
  [runtime observation](references/runtime-observation.md) for connect/launch
  and the focused follow-up browser tools.
- Fiddler Everywhere traffic or a native `.saz` capture: read the
  [Fiddler workflow](references/runtime-observation.md#fiddler-everywhere-traffic-debugging).
  Inspect saved SAZ with `inspect_web_network_capture` and `format: "saz"`;
  connect Everywhere's separate MCP server for live traffic.
- Retained HAR/SAZ/native mitmproxy/aioquic qlog capture: `inspect_web_network_capture`. Select
  original record ordinals when useful; inspect producer fields and byte/number
  sidecars without fetching recorded URLs or claiming live attribution. See
  [historical captures](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/web-network-captures.md) for the exact upstream
  profile and credential exclusions. Qlog support starts with aioquic 1.5.0
  JSON 0.3; stream coverage and endpoint loss declarations do not recover bodies
  or establish network loss. Prefer detail summary, then kind qlog trace/stream
  pages; select one trace, stream ID and direction for contribution/range pages.
  Facts retain all-recorded-events-before-selection scope. Other qlog layouts
  and PCAP correlation are unsupported.
- User-owned Electron runtime already open: `list_electron_targets`. Before an electron-main Inspector attempt, check packaged fuses with `inspect_electron_fuses`; disabled `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` means the app ignores `--inspect`.
- Packet-field discovery: `inspect_packet_fields` searches installed protocols
  and field names/types before choosing fields for `inspect_packet_capture`.
  Query/page the relevant records; registrations do not establish observed traffic.
- Recorded packet captures: `inspect_packet_capture` with selected TShark fields,
  display filters and decode-as rules. Requires Linux, util-linux prlimit and `REA_TSHARK_COMMAND`; see
  [capture guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/packet-captures.md).
  Packet limits count input packets before filtering. Output defaults to 50 matching
  frames; use `match_offset` / `match_limit` for later pages, or explicit null
  limit for complete matching output. Preserve the source digest across pages.
  This does not perform live capture.
  For address/DNS/SNI/protocol summaries use `inspect_pcap_capture` with MCP
  detail summary, then retained kind pcap pages. Requires Wireshark 4.x tshark
  and capinfos, with Linux prlimit or Windows Job Objects; see
  [packet summaries](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/pcap-analysis.md).
  Select an exact DNS question for address pages; page exhaustion does not prove
  network completeness. This reads recordings and does not acquire traffic.
- Decoder discovery: `inspect_signal_decoders` searches installed decoder IDs
  or selected decoder help, including channels and options. Query and page the
  relevant details before choosing settings; this does not scan hardware.
- Recorded logic/signal traces: `decode_signal_recording` with explicit decoder,
  channel and protocol settings. On Linux with util-linux prlimit, supply sigrok-cli 0.7.2 through
  `REA_SIGROK_COMMAND`; see [recording guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/signal-recordings.md).
  Output defaults to 50 literal lines; select annotation classes and page with
  `line_offset` / `line_limit`, or explicit null for all remaining output.
  Window counts are display lines, not annotations or samples. Preserve source digests across pages.
  This reads existing files; it does not acquire hardware signals.
- Explicit local WebAssembly artifact: `inspect_wasm_artifact`. Supply WABT 1.0.42
  through `REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY`; retain exact byte/tool identity and decoded WAT.
  Select JavaScript glue and candidate paths explicitly and preserve URL/path
  ambiguity. No implicit fetch or target execution; WAT is not original source.
  See the [WASM guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/wasm-artifacts.md).
- Explicit local EVM bytecode carrier: `inspect_evm_interface` with caller-selected
  `raw` or `hex` encoding. Preserve carrier/decoded digests and treat selectors,
  argument strings and mutability as inferred candidates; this performs no chain
  lookup or target execution. For the complete inferred interface without hex or
  duplicate stdout, discover support and select `detail: "summary"`; complete
  Evidence stays retained under its original identity. Use the returned
  `parent_evidence_id` for exact function or `bytecode_hex`/stdout/stderr pages.
  Candidate coverage does not establish interface completeness. See the
  [EVM bytecode guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/evm-bytecode.md).
- Embedded Go compiler, module or build-setting metadata: `inspect_go_binary`

  Go installation or disassembler. Preserve raw module bytes and source ranges;
  absent metadata does not prove a binary is not Go, and unparsed text records

  [Go binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/go-binaries.md).
- Embedded cargo-auditable Rust dependency metadata: `inspect_rust_binary`

  A rustc commit hash is an inference from a read-only `/rustc/<40-hex>/` path.
  See the
  [Rust binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/rust-binaries.md).

- Explicit local SQLite database snapshot: `inspect_sqlite_database`. Inspect

  report truncation and have unspecified order. Use a quiescent snapshot rather

  [SQLite guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/sqlite-databases.md).
- Explicit Linux ELF file for offline layout, symbols, relocations or static

  raw locations and inference/coverage limits; see the
  [offline binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/binary-diagnostics.md).
- Supplied Linux x86-64 ELF core: `inspect_recorded_crash`. Read every recorded
  thread, raw note and source-bound register without opening a live target.
  Historical PIDs do not select live processes. Request `include_debugger_context`

- PE resource type/name/language trees and static icon group references:

- Native executable, library, or analysis database: `open_binary`, then
  use focused analysis tools directly; call `binary_overview` when metadata or
  inventory context is useful and available from the selected provider.

## Work summary-first

Start with the default result and use its inline Evidence and graph context.
For a JavaScript application or ELF layout whose size is unknown or large,
call `analyze_javascript_application` or `inspect_binary_layout` with
`"detail": "summary"`, then inspect the retained `parent_evidence_id` with
`inspect_analysis_view`.
Page module identities and select the returned `node_id` before requesting an
item; a single file path can represent several graph roles. Do not repeat an
identical analysis or rejected call without a changed input or resolved blocker.
Recheck session state when a lifecycle change makes that status useful.
Make a focused follow-up only when the
returned result leaves a specific question unanswered.

If MCP reports `resource_constraint` with `details.resource: "transport"`, call

`retention: "complete-record"` means the whole record is stored; native
value-flow truncation and unknown metadata remain separate. For an exported
portable bundle, use `rea inspect-evidence-bundle` with JSON containing `path`,
`detail: "summary"` and the same `filters`. Reading that file still requires
validating its full contents within the local memory budget.

A client can also truncate a successful tool result without a REA transport
error. Treat that preview as incomplete; use the retained parent ID for smaller
views or export when the full record is needed. Do not parse the preview as
canonical JSON or repeat the producer. For JavaScript, read the
[module-view and trace recipes](references/javascript-applications.md) before
drilling into a large graph; a broad bidirectional trace can expand unrelated
containment relationships even after summary analysis.

Every conclusion must distinguish observations, inferences, and unknowns. Cite
Evidence IDs, preserve limitations and incomplete coverage, and never imply
that static analysis observed execution. Runtime requests execute the declared
target and lifecycle; do not broaden the target or action beyond those fields.

Within the user's requested investigation, call available analysis tools
directly. REA does not require permission grants or per-call approval flags.
The agent client can independently require approval. Follow the declared request
scope and the host's actual access requirements; use the recovery guide for an
observed client-policy rejection.

## Plan broader investigations

For requests that span multiple features or subsystems, use a staged workflow:

1. Turn the request into a checklist of questions and the evidence each answer
   needs. Resolve target identity and constraints from the conversation and
   workspace before asking for information again.
2. Inspect the current REA session, artifact identity, saved analysis database,
   bookmarks, and prior evidence. Reuse matching state; do not open duplicate
   sessions or repeat identical analysis.
3. Start with the smallest useful overview or inventory. Follow each question
   from its entry point through relevant data and state changes to its result.
   Batch related operations around a specific hypothesis, then expand only when
   the returned evidence leaves a concrete gap.
4. Inspect relevant packaged resources and configuration alongside code when
   they affect the question. Use format-aware inventory and parsers; do not
   infer behavior from filenames, strings, or layout alone.
5. Corroborate a conclusion with the evidence type it requires. Use runtime
   observation only when static evidence cannot answer the question and the
   required host runtime and OS access are available. For JavaScript behavior,
   run probes against the actual app through the available browser, Electron,
   or process capture workflow.
6. Decompose work into independent questions. When parallel workers are
   available and the questions do not depend on one another, assign distinct
   scopes, point workers to existing evidence, and ask them to return sources,
   conclusions, and unresolved gaps. Otherwise, work sequentially.
7. Keep a concise finding ledger linking each conclusion to Evidence IDs,
   confidence/evidence type, search boundary, and remaining unknowns. Update
   the shared index or investigation report so later passes can reuse results.

Before finishing, revisit the original checklist. Mark each question as
answered, partially answered, or unresolved based on its evidence; keep
bounded negative searches bounded, and do not describe a broad investigation
as complete while required questions remain open.

## What the software is (observed)

**Stack**
- `CardLock.Exe` — PE32 x86, **native, not .NET** (REA: *"The PE has no CLI data directory"*), Borland **Delphi 7** VCL + Tnt Unicode controls (`d:\program files (x86)\borland\delphi7\Lib\Tnt*.pas` in the binary).
- Data access via **DevArt DAC** (`DAC\Common\Source\CR*.pas`) with **BDE**, **OLE DB** and **MySQL** providers — `libmysql.dll`, `IDAPI32.DLL`, `xolehlp.dll` all shipped.
- `CardLock.mdb` — Access DB, **password-protected** (both Jet 4.0 and ACE report *"Not a valid password"*), so the app supplies a DB password at runtime.
- Skinning: `mxskin*.skn`; reports: Excel templates (`ReportGuests.xls`, `ReportCards.xls`, `ReportOpen.xls`).

**Card hardware layer** (the interesting part)
- `proRFL.dll` — the card-model API: `GuestCard`, `MasterCard`, `EmergencyCard`, `FloorCard`, `GroupCard`, `GroupSetCard`, `BuildingCard`, `CheckOutCard`, `LimitCard`, `IniCard`, `RoomSetCard`, `RecordCard`, `ReadCard`, `ReadRecord`, `CardErase`, `ResetCard`, `DirectReadUSB`, `DirectWriteUSB`, `initializeUSB`, `IniUsb`, `IniUsbPro`, `ReadE2`, `readPortb`, `readPortPro`.
- `Mwic_32.dll` — magnetic stripe track 1/2/3 (`Read_45`/`Write_45`, `srd_eeprom`/`swr_eeprom`) plus `DES_Encrypt`/`DES_Decrypt`, `ic_encrypt`/`ic_decrypt`.
- `d12.dll` (raw USB via `SetupDi*` + `DeviceIoControl`) and `d12c.dll` (MFC wrapper — explains the shipped `MFC42D.DLL`/`MSVCRTD.DLL`).
- Custom port protocol: `readPorta/readPortb/writePorta/writePortb` — the card encoder is driven byte-wise over a USB port, not a standard smartcard API.

**Domain model** (from VCL component names): rooms/buildings, guest lifecycle (`CheckOutByCard`, `CloseGuest`, `CheckOutNoCard`), card issuance for guest/master/floor/group/building/emergency/blacklist types, `CardErase`, `CardInfo`, lock clock sync (`cmdClockSetting`), lock config (`cmdLocksConfiguration`). `Reg.ini`/`System.ini` hold reader identity (`proM9-20121130-14`, `proUSB20140107`), dongle-ish `SN`/`Days`/`SA`/`SB`/`SC` values.

- Parse DOS header e_lfanew at 0x3C.

- Walk directory: 16-byte entries: Name/ID (4), OffsetToData(4, high bit = subdirectory), ...

Let me rewrite the DFM parser properly with a clean recursive design:

DFM binary format:
- Signature "TPF0"
- Then one or more objects (usually just one, but a form is a single root object).

Object:
- ClassName: short string (1-byte length + chars, Pascal shortstring)
- ObjectName: short string
- Property list: sequence of (PropName shortstring, Value) terminated by 0x00
- Then children: sequence of objects, terminated by 0x00

Value:
- vaNull=0: nothing (used as terminator in lists)
- vaList=1: '(' then values... terminated by vaNull(0), then ')'
- vaInt8=2, vaInt16=3, vaInt32=4
- vaExtended=5 (10 bytes)
- vaString=6: shortstring
- vaIdent=7: shortstring
- vaFalse=8, vaTrue=9
- vaBinary=10: int32 length + bytes
- vaSet=11: sequence of shortstrings terminated by 0
- vaLString=12: int32 length + bytes
- vaNil=13
- vaCollection=14: '(' then objects terminated by 0
- vaSingle=15 (4 bytes)
- vaCurrency=16 (8)
- vaDate=17 (8)
- vaWString=18: int32 char count + UTF-16 chars
- vaInt64=19 (8)
- vaUTF8String=20: int32 byte count + bytes
- vaDouble=21 (8)

Lists can be nested arbitrarily (e.g., Font.Style = [fsBold] is a set, Items.Strings = ('a' 'b') is a list of strings).

i < numSections; i++) {\n    sections.push({\n      va: buf.readUInt32LE(secOff + 12),\n      vsize: buf.readUInt32LE(secOff + 8),\n      rawSize: buf.readUInt32LE(secOff + 16),\n      rawPtr: buf.readUInt32LE(secOff + 20),\n    });\n    secOff += 40;\n  }\n  const rvaToOff = (rva) => {\n    for (const s of sections) {\n      if (rva >= s.va && rva < s.va + Math.max(s.vsize, s.rawSize)) return rva - s.va + s.rawPtr;\n    }\n    return -1;\n  };\n  const cstr = (off) => {\n    if (off < 0) return \"?\";\n    let end = off;\n    while (end < buf.length && buf[end] !== 0) end++;\n    return buf.toString(\"latin1\", off, end);\n  };\n\n  console.log(`\\n=== ${basename(file)} ===`);\n  const machine = buf.readUInt16LE(peOff + 4);\n  console.log(`machine=0x${machine.toString(16)}  size=${buf.length}`);\n\n  // exports\n  const expRva = buf.readUInt32LE(ddOff + 0 * 8);\n  if (!expRva) {\n    console.log(\"exports: none\");\n  } else {\n    const e = rvaToOff(expRva);\n    const nameRva = buf.readUInt32LE(e + 12);\n    const ordinalBase = buf.readUInt32LE(e + 16);\n    const numNames = buf.readUInt32LE(e + 24);\n    const namesRva = buf.readUInt32LE(e + 32);\n    const ordRva = buf.readUInt32LE(e + 36);\n    console.log(`exports: ${numNames} named  (dll: ${cstr(rvaToOff(nameRva))})`);\n    const out = [];\n    for (let i = 0; i < numNames; i++) {\n      const nOff = rvaToOff(buf.readUInt32LE(rvaToOff(namesRva) + i * 4));\n      const ord = buf.readUInt16LE(rvaToOff(ordRva) + i * 2);\n      out.push(`${ord + ordinalBase}  ${cstr(nOff)}`);\n    }\n    for (const line of out) console.log(\"  \" + line);\n  }\n\n  // imports (DLL names only)\n  const impRva = buf.readUInt32LE(ddOff + 1 * 8);\n  if (impRva) {\n    const dlls = [];\n    let d = rvaToOff(impRva);\n    for (;;) {\n      const oft = buf.readUInt32LE(d);\n      const nameRva2 = buf.readUInt32LE(d + 12);\n      const ft = buf.readUInt32LE(d + 16);\n      if (!oft && !nameRva2 && !ft) break;\n      dlls.push(cstr(rvaToOff(nameRva2)));\n      d += 20;\n      if (dlls.length > 200) break;\n    }\n    console.log(\"imports: \" + dlls.join(\", \"));\n  }\n}\n",

What the encoder is\n\n| Mode | Device | Driver | API |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Legacy | AVR USB device (`D:\\avr-usb\\d12\\d12.cpp`) | vendor kernel driver installed by the setup | `d12.dll` → `DeviceIoControl(IOCTL 0x22200C)` |\n| **Pro** | **USB HID**, `VID 0x9915` / `PID 0x1116` | none (Windows HID) | `d12c.dll` → HID output report `0x40` |\n\nThe application picks the mode with `initializeUSB(0)` (legacy) or `initializeUSB(1)` (HID) and\npasses the same flag to every card function.\n\n## 2. Is the encoder present?\n\n```powershell\nGet-PnpDevice -PresentOnly |\n  Where-Object { $_.InstanceId -match 'VID_9915' -or $_.InstanceId -match 'PID_1116' } |\n  Format-List Status, Class, FriendlyName, InstanceId\n```\n\nAt the time of this analysis **no such device was present** on the machine — the encoder was not\nplugged in, so nothing below has been exercised against hardware.\n\n## 3. Wire format (recap)\n\nEvery card write is one 64-byte transfer:\n\n```\nAA 21 EC | 32 payload bytes | XOR checksum | zero padding\n                             ^ 0x67 ^ payload[0..31]\n```\n\nHID framing adds the report ID:\n\n```\nreport[0]    = 0x40\nreport[1..63]= frame (padded with 0x00)\nWriteFile(handle, report, OutputReportByteLength)\n```\n\nReads are the mirror image: one input report, 63 payload bytes, 2 s timeout.\n\n## 4. Commissioning sequence (as the vendor UI describes it)\n\n1. **Reset Card** — `IniCard(port, mode, out)`, mode `0` / `1` / `2`, frame `AA 01 96 3D`,\n   `AA 01 69 C2` or `AA 01 56 FD`; the lock answers with a 36-byte response.\n2. **RoomNo. Setting** — `RoomSetCard(...)`, record byte 9 = `0x20 + n`.\n3. **Lock Clock Setting** — `TimeSetCard(...)`, record byte 9 = `0x30 + n`.\n\nThen guest/master cards (`0x60 + n`, `0xB0 + n`) are accepted by the lock.\n\n## 5. Minimal HID harness (Python)\n\n```python\n# pip install hidapi\nimport hid\n\nVID, PID = 0x9915, 0x1116\n\ndef open_encoder():\n    for d in hid.enumerate(VID, PID):\n        # usage_page/usage distinguish the vendor collection from keyboard/mouse ones\n        dev = hid.device()\n        dev.open_path(d[\"path\"])\n        return dev\n    raise SystemExit(\"encoder not found\")\n\ndef xor_checksum(payload32: bytes) -> int:\n    c = 0x67\n    for b in payload32:\n        c ^= b\n    return c & 0xFF\n\ndef frame(payload32: bytes) -> bytes:\n    assert len(payload32) == 32\n    body = bytes([0xAA, 0x21, 0xEC]) + payload32 + bytes([xor_checksum(payload32)])\n    return body.ljust(63, b\"\\x00\")\n\ndef write_card(dev, payload32: bytes):\n    report = bytes([0x40]) + frame(payload32)      # 64 bytes\n    dev.write(report)\n\ndef read_card(dev) -> bytes:\n    data = dev.read(64, timeout_ms=2000)           # strips nothing: check your hidapi build\n    return bytes(data[1:64])                       # skip report ID\n```\n\n`hid.device.write` prepends nothing; the first byte of the buffer **is** the report ID, which is\nwhy `report[0] = 0x40`. If your `hidapi` build expects a different convention, the device will\nsimply not answer — verify with a read after the write.\n\n## 6. Replaying an existing card (safest first test)\n\nThe database already stores 16-byte records (`CardInfo.CardData`, 32 hex chars). A card whose\nrecord was issued by this system can be reproduced without rebuilding the field semantics:\n\n```python\nrec16 = bytes.fromhex(\"C9120000FF00298000B1881BC2F81DFB\")   # CardInfo.CardData\npayload32 = rec16 + bytes(16)                                # see CARD-API.md §9 (length open item)\nwrite_card(dev, payload32)\n```\n\nThis is the quickest way to confirm the transport, checksum and report framing on real hardware\nbefore generating new records.\n\n## 7. Verifying a write\n\n1. `write_card(...)` must not raise.\n2. Immediately `read_card(...)`: the lock/encoder echoes a 36-byte response for `IniCard`; for\n   record writes the reply is the device status.\n3. Present the card to a lock you administer and use the vendor UI's *Card Info* / *Record* read to\n   confirm the record matches `CardInfo.CardData`.\n\n## 8. Caveats\n\n* The legacy path needs the vendor's kernel driver; the HID path does not.\n* Windows may hold the HID device exclusively while `CardLock.Exe` is running — close it first.\n* The 4 bytes after the 16-byte record and the exact meaning of several packed fields are still\n  unresolved (`CARD-API.md` §9); do not assume a generated record is valid until a lock accepts it.\n",
  "path": "C:\\Users\\gzers\\AndroidStudioProjects\\Appointment\\docs\\re-proUSB\\ENCODER.md"
}
```

The main one is the record-length mismatch (20 bytes built, 32 bytes\ntransmitted, 16 bytes stored), which can only be settled by decompiling `CardLock.Exe` and reading\nthe call sites.\n\n## Legal / ethical scope\n\nThis dossier documents software installed on the machine it was analysed on, for interoperability\nwith locks the owner administers. ## Ce que l'analyse a établi (vérifié dans le code décompilé)

**Format carte** — enregistrement de 16 octets, trame `AA 21 EC` + 32 octets + checksum XOR (graine `0x67`), transfert de 64 octets.

**Octet 9 = type | index** — table complète recoupée avec la base elle-même (les 44 cartes `0xB0–0xBF` et les 8 cartes `0x60–0x6F` correspondent exactement) :

```
0x1n record   0x2n RoomNo setting   0x3n horloge   0x4n limite   0x5n group-set
0x6n client   0x7n checkout         0x8n groupe    0xAn urgence  0xBn master
0xCn bâtiment 0xDn étage
```

**Encodeur** — deux transports, choisis par `initializeUSB(0|1)` :
- **Pro (HID)** : `d12c.dll`, VID `0x9915` / PID `0x1116`, report de sortie `0x40`, 63 octets utiles, lecture en overlapped avec timeout 2 s.
- **Legacy** : `d12.dll`, périphérique AVR USB, `DeviceIoControl` IOCTL `0x22200C` (buffer unique entrée/sortie).

**Mise en service** (ordre confirmé par l'UI et le code) : Reset Card (`IniCard`, `AA 01 69 C2` / `AA 01 96 3D` / `AA 01 56 FD`) → RoomNo. Setting → Lock Clock Setting.

**Exemple réel décodé** (`C9120000FF00298000B1881BC2F81DFB`, ID 3) : master, index 1, `param_6 = 8`, et deux groupes de dates lisibles **2015-08-03** et **2023-08-03 23:59**.

## Non vérifié / limites

1. **L'encodeur n'était pas branché** pendant l'analyse (aucun `VID_9915` présent) — le protocole n'a donc jamais été exercé sur matériel.
2. **Incohérence de longueur** : les constructeurs appellent `hex_a(..., 0x14)` (20 octets), `WriteCard` émet 32 octets, la base stocke 16 octets. Seule la décompilation de `CardLock.Exe` (4 Mo, non faite) tranchera.
3. **Encodage d'entrée des cartes client** (`GuestCard` soustrait `0x80` à trois champs) — non résolu sans l'appelant EXE.
4. **16 lignes `CardInfo` anormales** (octet 9 = `0x01,0x08,0x0A,0x0B,0x0F,0x1D,0x1E`) hors table de types.
5. Signification de `param_2` (24 bits) et des champs `M`/`O` encore inconnue.

## Risques

- Le dossier décrit une installation possédée ; il ne contient **aucun secret** (mot de passe base uniquement dans `tools/re-proUSB/local.env`, git-ignoré et non commité — vérifié par scan du diff indexé).
- Aucun code applicatif modifié, donc aucun impact sur les builds.
- L'analyse est strictement statique : pas de génération de clés, pas d'exécution du logiciel.

`docs/HEALTH.md` laissé à **100/100** : le travail est documentaire, l'état de l'application est inchangé (le run CI du commit le confirme).

I'll add to C#:

```csharp
public static string SendAndRead(string path, byte[] frame, int sendDelayMs, int readTimeoutMs, int inLen)
{
    IntPtr hw = CreateFile(path, GENERIC_WRITE, FILE_SHARE_RW, IntPtr.Zero, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, IntPtr.Zero);
    if (hw == INVALID) return "ERROR=open_write:" + Marshal.GetLastWin32Error();

    IntPtr hr = CreateFile(path, 0x80000000, FILE_SHARE_RW, IntPtr.Zero, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, IntPtr.Zero);

    try
    {
        byte[] report = new byte[65];
        report[0] = 0x40;
        Array.Copy(frame, 0, report, 1, Math.Min(frame.Length, 63));

        int written = 0;
        if (!WriteFile(hw, report, 65, out written, IntPtr.Zero))
            return "ERROR=WriteFile:" + Marshal.GetLastWin32Error();

        System.Threading.Thread.Sleep(sendDelayMs);

        if (hr == INVALID) return "WROTE=" + written + "|ERROR=open_read:" + Marshal.GetLastWin32Error();

        IntPtr ev = CreateEvent(IntPtr.Zero, true, false, IntPtr.Zero);
        try
        {
            byte[] buf = new byte[inLen];
            OVERLAPPED ov = new OVERLAPPED();
            ov.hEvent = ev;
            bool started = ReadFile(hr, buf, inLen, IntPtr.Zero, ref ov);
            int err = Marshal.GetLastWin32Error();
            if (!started && err != 997) return "WROTE=" + written + "|ERROR=ReadFile:" + err;

            uint wait = WaitForSingleObject(ev, (uint)readTimeoutMs);
            if (wait == 258) { CancelIo(hr); return "WROTE=" + written + "|RESULT=timeout"; }
            if (wait != 0) return "WROTE=" + written + "|RESULT=wait:" + wait;

            int tr = 0;
            if (!GetOverlappedResult(hr, ref ov, out tr, false))
                return "WROTE=" + written + "|ERROR=GetOverlappedResult:" + Marshal.GetLastWin32Error();

            return "WROTE=" + written + "|RESULT=ok|BYTES=" + tr + "|DATA=" + Hex(buf, tr);
        }
        finally { CloseHandle(ev); }
    }
    finally
    {
        CloseHandle(hw);
        if (hr != INVALID) CloseHandle(hr);
    }
}
```

Note: the report length must equal OutputReportByteLength (65). Good.

1: # Driving the card encoder
2: 
3: > Practical notes for re-using the installed proUSB encoder with your own tooling.
4: > Only for locks you own or administer.
5: 
6: ## 1. What the encoder is
7: 
8: | Mode | Device | Driver | API |
9: |---|---|---|---|
10: | Legacy | AVR USB device (`D:\avr-usb\d12\d12.cpp`) | vendor kernel driver installed by the setup | `d12.dll` → `DeviceIoControl(IOCTL 0x22200C)` |
11: | **Pro** | **USB HID**, `VID 0x9915` / `PID 0x1116` | none (Windows HID) | `d12c.dll` → HID output report `0x40` |
12: 
13: The application picks the mode with `initializeUSB(0)` (legacy) or `initializeUSB(1)` (HID) and
14: passes the same flag to every card function.
15: 
16: ## 2. Is the encoder present?
17: 
18: ```powershell
19: Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly |
20:   Where-Object { $_.InstanceId -match 'VID_9915' -or $_.InstanceId -match 'PID_1116' } |
21:   Format-List Status, Class, FriendlyName, InstanceId
22: ```
23: 
24: At the time of this analysis **no such device was present** on the machine — the encoder was not
25: plugged in, so nothing below has been exercised against hardware.
26: 
27: ## 3. Wire format (recap)
28: 
29: Every card write is one 64-byte transfer:
30: 
31: ```
32: AA 21 EC | 32 payload bytes | XOR checksum | zero padding
33:                              ^ 0x67 ^ payload[0..31]
34: ```
35: 
36: HID framing adds the report ID:
37: 
38: ```
39: report[0]    = 0x40
40: report[1..63]= frame (padded with 0x00)
41: WriteFile(handle, report, OutputReportByteLength)
42: ```
43: 
44: Reads are the mirror image: one input report, 63 payload bytes, 2 s timeout.
45: 
46: ## 4. Commissioning sequence (as the vendor UI describes it)
47: 
48: 1. **Reset Card** — `IniCard(port, mode, out)`, mode `0` / `1` / `2`, frame `AA 01 96 3D`,
49:    `AA 01 69 C2` or `AA 01 56 FD`; the lock answers with a 36-byte response.
50: 2. **RoomNo. Setting** — `RoomSetCard(...)`, record byte 9 = `0x20 + n`.
51: 3. **Lock Clock Setting** — `TimeSetCard(...)`, record byte 9 = `0x30 + n`.
52: 
53: Then guest/master cards (`0x60 + n`, `0xB0 + n`) are accepted by the lock.
54: 
55: ## 5. Minimal HID harness (Python)
56: 
57: ```python
58: # pip install hidapi
59: import hid
60: 
61: VID, PID = 0x9915, 0x1116
62: 
63: def open_encoder():
64:     for d in hid.enumerate(VID, PID):
65:         # usage_page/usage distinguish the vendor collection from keyboard/mouse ones
66:         dev = hid.device()
67:         dev.open_path(d["path"])
68:         return dev
69:     raise SystemExit("encoder not found")
70: 
71: def xor_checksum(payload32: bytes) -> int:
72:     c = 0x67
73:     for b in payload32:
74:         c ^= b
75:     return c & 0xFF
76: 
77: def frame(payload32: bytes) -> bytes:
78:     assert len(payload32) == 32
79:     body = bytes([0xAA, 0x21, 0xEC]) + payload32 + bytes([xor_checksum(payload32)])
80:     return body.ljust(63, b"\x00")
81: 
82: def write_card(dev, payload32: bytes):
83:     report = bytes([0x40]) + frame(payload32)      # 64 bytes
84:     dev.write(report)
85: 
86: def read_card(dev) -> bytes:
87:     data = dev.read(64, timeout_ms=2000)           # strips nothing: check your hidapi build
88:     return bytes(data[1:64])                       # skip report ID
89: ```
90: 
91: `hid.device.write` prepends nothing; the first byte of the buffer **is** the report ID, which is
92: why `report[0] = 0x40`. If your `hidapi` build expects a different convention, the device will
93: simply not answer — verify with a read after the write.
94: 
95: ## 6. Replaying an existing card (safest first test)
96: 
97: The database already stores 16-byte records (`CardInfo.CardData`, 32 hex chars). A card whose
98: record was issued by this system can be reproduced without rebuilding the field semantics:
99: 
100: ```python
101: rec16 = bytes.fromhex("C9120000FF00298000B1881BC2F81DFB")   # CardInfo.CardData
102: payload32 = rec16 + bytes(16)                                # see CARD-API.md §9 (length open item)
103: write_card(dev, payload32)
104: ```
105: 
106: This is the quickest way to confirm the transport, checksum and report framing on real hardware
107: before generating new records.
108: 
109: ## 7. Verifying a write
110: 
111: 1. `write_card(...)` must not raise.
112: 2. Immediately `read_card(...)`: the lock/encoder echoes a 36-byte response for `IniCard`; for
113:    record writes the reply is the device status.
114: 3. Present the card to a lock you administer and use the vendor UI's *Card Info* / *Record* read to
115:    confirm the record matches `CardInfo.CardData`.
116: 
117: ## 8. Caveats
118: 
119: * The legacy path needs the vendor's kernel driver; the HID path does not.
120: * Windows may hold the HID device exclusively while `CardLock.Exe` is running — close it first.
121: * The 4 bytes after the 16-byte record and the exact meaning of several packed fields are still
122:   unresolved (`CARD-API.md` §9); do not assume a generated record is valid until a lock accepts it.

151: where `d8`, `d9`, `d10` are decimal digit strings read as 2-character pairs.
152: 
153: ```
154: p8[2..3] -> A      p9[0..1] -> I     p10[2..3] -> E
155: p8[4..5] -> B      p9[2..3] -> J     p10[4..5] -> F
156: p8[6..7] -> C                        p10[6..7] -> G
157: p8[8..9] -> D                        p10[8..9] -> H
158: p8[0..1] -> M = (value - 9) & 0x0F
159: p10[0..1]-> O = (value - 9) & 0x0F
160: ```
161: 
162: | Byte | Expression |
163: |---|---|
164: | 4 | `param_7` (minus `0x80` when `param_5 != 0`) |
165: | 5 | `(J / 10) + I * 8` |
166: | 6 | `rand() & 0xFF` **(random nonce)** |
167: | 7 | `param_6 << 4` |
168: | 8 | `param_4` |
169: | 9 | `0xB0 \| (param_3 & 0x0F)` |
170: | 10 | `((M & 0x0F) << 4) \| A` |
171: | 11 | `(C >> 2) \| (B << 3)` |
172: | 12 | `((C & 3) << 6) \| D` |
173: | 13 | `((O & 0x0F) << 4) \| E` |
174: | 14 | `(G >> 2) \| (F << 3)` |
175: | 15 | `((G & 3) << 6) \| H` |
176: 
177: Decoding a real row (`CardData = C9120000FF00298000B1881BC2F81DFB`, `ID=3`):
178: 
179: | Field | Value |
180: |---|---|
181: | bytes 0–3 | `C9 12 00 00` |
182: | byte 4 (`param_7`) | `0xFF` |
183: | byte 5 | `0x00` → `I = 0`, `J < 10` |
184: | byte 6 | `0x29` → random nonce |
185: | byte 7 | `0x80` → `param_6 = 8` |
186: | byte 8 (`param_4`) | `0x00` |
187: | byte 9 | `0xB1` → MasterCard, index 1 |
188: | byte 10 | `0x88` → `M = 8`, `A = 8` |
189: | byte 11 | `0x1B` → `B = 3`, `C >> 2 = 3` |
190: | byte 12 | `0xC2` → `C & 3 = 3` ⇒ `C = 15`, `D = 2` |
191: | byte 13 | `0xF8` → `O = 15`, `E = 8` |
192: | byte 14 | `0x1D` → `F = 3`, `G >> 2 = 5` |
193: | byte 15 | `0xFB` → `G & 3 = 3` ⇒ `G = 23`, `H = 59` |
194: 
195: Reading the two groups as timestamps gives **2015‑08‑03** and **2023‑08‑03 23:59** — consistent
196: with a validity window (**inferred**: start / end). `M` and `O` are two extra 4-bit fields whose
197: meaning is **unknown** (weekday, card counter, or part of a checksum).
198: 
199: ### 7.3 GuestCard (**verified**)
200: 
201: Same head, `0x3B = 0x60 + (param_3 & 0x0F)`, and:
202: 
203: | Byte | Expression |
204: |---|---|
205: | 4 | `L - 0x80` (only when `param_5 != 0`) |
206: | 5 | `K - 0x80` |
207: | 6 | `J - 0x80` |
208: | 7 | `param_6 << 4 \| (I & 0x0F)` |
209: | 8 | `param_4` |
210: | 10–15 | same bit-packing as MasterCard, fed from `p7/p8/p9` |
211: 
212: Because the caller subtracts `0x80` from three decimal-derived bytes, a valid guest card requires
213: those inputs to be ≥ 0x80 once offset — the EXE therefore does **not** pass plain decimal digits
214: here (**inferred**; the exact encoding lives in the EXE caller, see §9).
215: 
216: ### 7.4 RoomSetCard (**verified**)
217: 
218: ```
219: 0x3B = 0x20 + (param_3 & 0x0F)
220: byte 4 = p7[0..1] pair      byte 5 = p7[2..3]
221: byte 6 = p7[4..5]           byte 7 = param_5<<4 | (p6[0..1] & 0x0F)
222: byte 8 = param_4            byte 9 = (param_3 & 0x0F) + 0x20
223: byte 10 = ((p6[0..1]-9)&0xF)<<4 | p6[2..3]
224: byte 11 = (C>>2) | (B<<3)   byte 12 = ((C&3)<<6) | D
225: byte 13..15 = rand()        (random nonce)
226: ```
227: 
228: ### 7.5 TimeSetCard (**verified**)
229: 
230: `0x3B = (param_3 & 0x0F) + 0x30`; bytes 4–7 are `rand()`; byte 8 = `param_4`;
231: byte 9 = `0x30 + n`; byte 10 = `(p6[0..1]-9)<<4 | p6[2..3]`; bytes 11–12 = packed `p6` pairs;
232: byte 13 = `param_5 & 7`; bytes 14–15 = `rand()`.
233: 
234: ### 7.6 Other types
235: 
236: `FloorCard`, `BuildingCard`, `GroupCard`, `EmergencyCard`, `CheckOutCard`, `LimitCard`,
237: `GroupSetCard`, `RecordCard` all use the same `0xC9` + type-byte scheme; their per-field packing
238: was not fully transcribed. `CardErase`, `ResetCard`, `CloseCard` and `IniCard` use a **different,
239: shorter frame** (`AA …` command frames, no `0xC9` record).
240: 
241: ## 8. `IniCard` — lock initialisation (**verified**)
242: 
243: ```c
244: frame = { 0xAA, 0x01, m0, m1 }      /* 4 bytes */
245: m0,m1 = { 0x69,0xC2 }  when mode == 1
246:         { 0x96,0x3D }  when mode == 0
247:         { 0x56,0xFD }  when mode == 2
248: 
249: write_port(port, 0x40, frame);
250: if (port == 0) read_port(port, 0x40, resp);   /* legacy only */
251: Sleep(mode == 2 ? 100 : 1200);
252: read_port(port, 0x40, resp);
253: hex_a(resp, out, 0x24);                       /* 36-byte response → 72 hex chars */
254: ```
255: 
256: This is the **Reset Card** step of the commissioning sequence.
257: 
258: ## 9. Open items
259: 
260: 1. **Record length discrepancy.** Builders call `hex_a(record, out, 0x14)` (20 bytes → 40 hex
261:    chars) while `WriteCard` transmits `0x20` (32) payload bytes, and the database stores exactly
262:    16 bytes (32 hex chars). The EXE caller therefore truncates and/or owns a 32-byte struct.
263:    Resolution requires decompiling `CardLock.Exe` and reading the call sites.
264: 2. **Guest card input encoding** (§7.3) — needs the EXE caller.
265: 3. **16 anomalous `CardInfo` rows** (byte 9 = `0x01,0x08,0x0A,0x0B,0x0F,0x1D,0x1E`, prefixes
266:    `C912033B / C912169A / C912316A`) that do not fit the type table. Probably records produced by
267:    an older build or a different card family.
268: 4. **`param_2` (24-bit site/serial)** and the numeric meaning of `A…H`, `M`, `O`.
269: 5. The encoder was **not connected** during this analysis (no `VID_9915` HID device present), so
270:    no live handshake was observed.

## 5. Frame format (**verified**)

`WriteCard(port, record)` wraps the record in a fixed frame:

```
offset 0   AA
offset 1   21
offset 2   EC
offset 3.. 34  payload (32 bytes copied from the record buffer)
offset 35  XOR checksum = 0x67 ^ payload[0] ^ payload[1] ^ … ^ payload[31]
           (total 36 meaningful bytes; the 64-byte transfer is zero-padded on the HID path)
```

The transfer length is **64 bytes** (`write_port(port, 0x40, frame)`).

80: ### 4.2 Write (`writePortPro` → `FUN_10001a60`) (**verified on hardware**)
81: 
82: The decompiled order of the two first statements is a debug-build dead store: the report ID is
83: written and then zeroed.
84: 
85: ```c
86: BYTE report[65];
87: DAT_10132d80 = 0x40;              /* HID report ID …                      */
88: memset(&DAT_10132d80, 0, 0x41);   /* … immediately overwritten with 0x00  */
89: memcpy(&DAT_10132d81, frame, 63); /* 63-byte payload at offset 1          */
90: WriteFile(hWrite, report, OutputReportByteLength, &written, NULL);
91: ```
92: 
93: Report ID `0x40` is the one that actually drives the device: three buzzer frames sent with it
94: produced three audible beeps (§4.4). `WriteFile` also accepts `0x00` and even `0x41`, so a
95: successful write is not proof of anything — only the buzzer or a card read-back is.
96: 
97: ### 4.3 Read (`readPortPro` → `FUN_100018c0`) (**verified on hardware**)
98: 
99: * read handle: `CreateFileA(path, GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ|WRITE, NULL, OPEN_EXISTING,
100:   FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, NULL)` — opening with access `0` fails with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (5)`
101: * manual-reset event + overlapped `ReadFile`, then `WaitForSingleObject(event, 2000)` → 2 s timeout
102: * one input report is **65 bytes**: `report[0]` is the report ID (`0x00` on this device) and the
103:   useful payload starts at `report[1]`; `d12c.dll` copies from `&DAT_10132d3c + 1`, i.e. it skips
104:   byte 0 and hands 63 bytes to the caller
105: 
106: ### 4.4 Hardware validation (**verified**)
107: 
108: Measured against the installed encoder (`USB\VID_9915&PID_1116\READER_0000016`):
109: 
110: | Property | Value |
111: |---|---|
112: | `HidD_GetAttributes` | VID `0x9915`, PID `0x1116`, version `0x0120` |
113: | Usage Page / Usage | `0x85FF` (vendor) / `0x0000` |
114: | `InputReportByteLength` | 65 |
115: | `OutputReportByteLength` | 65 |
116: | `FeatureReportByteLength` | 0 |
117: | Manufacturer | `Card Lock TEMIC_PRAD` |
118: | Product | `proUSB-TEMIC` |
119: | Serial | `Reader_0000016` |
120: 
121: Exercised commands:
122: 
123: | Command | Frame | Observed result |
124: |---|---|---|
125: | `Buzzer` on / off | `AA 02 80 01 29` / `AA 02 80 00 28` | **three distinct beeps**, send path proven |
126: | `ReadCard` | `AA 01 E4 4F` | `55 15 01 <20 bytes> <xor>` + `0xFF` padding, byte-for-byte reproducible |
127: | `WriteCard` | `AA 21 EC …` | no reply (nominal — `WriteCard` never reads); card content confirmed by read-back |
128: | `ReadRecord` | `AA 01 82 29` | no reply on a master card |
129: | `IniCard` 0 / 1 / 2 | `AA 01 96 3D` / `69 C2` / `56 FD` | no reply on a master card |
130: 
131: `IOCTL_HID_GET_REPORT_DESCRIPTOR` (`0x000B0000`) returns `ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION (1)` on this
132: device and Windows exposes no `ReportDescriptor` registry value, so the descriptor itself could not
133: be dumped. Report lengths are taken from `HidP_GetCaps`.
134: 
135: The device also **re-enumerates intermittently**: roughly one probe in three finds no matching
136: interface for a few hundred milliseconds, so every hardware call needs a retry loop.

145: offset 2   EC

# Ce que le test matériel a établi

L'encodeur branché est bien celui que le binaire attendait, et **tout le protocole est maintenant vérifié sur la carte**, plus seulement déduit du décompilé.

| Élément | Valeur mesurée |
|---|---|
| PnP | `USB\VID_9915&PID_1116\READER_0000016` |
| VID / PID / bcd | `0x9915` / `0x1116` / `0x0120` |
| Usage Page | `0x85FF` (vendor) |
| Rapports | **65 octets** entrée **et** sortie |
| Chaînes | `Card Lock TEMIC_PRAD` / `proUSB-TEMIC` / `Reader_0000016` |

**Une seule règle de checksum pour toutes les trames : le dernier octet = XOR de tous les précédents.** Le `0x67` de `WriteCard` n'est que la valeur initiale de l'accumulateur.

| Commande | Trame | Résultat observé |
|---|---|---|
| `Buzzer` | `AA 02 80 01 29` | **3 bips audibles** → le chemin d'écriture et le report ID `0x40` sont prouvés |
| `ReadCard` | `AA 01 E4 4F` | `55 15 01 …` reproductible octet pour octet |
| `WriteCard` | `AA 21 EC` + 32 + XOR | **aucune réponse, et c'est normal** : la fonction décompilée n'appelle jamais `readPort` |
| `ReadRecord` | `AA 01 82 29` | silence sur une carte master |
| `IniCard` 0/1/2 | `AA 01 96 3D` / `69 C2` / `56 FD` | silence sur une carte master |

Le silence de `WriteCard` n'était donc pas un échec : la preuve se fait par relecture.

# Le point important : la taille d'enregistrement est résolue

La carte contient une zone de **20 octets** :

```
55 15 01 | <16 octets d'enregistrement> | <4 octets calculés par le lecteur> | <xor>
```

Les 16 premiers octets sont exactement ce que la base stocke dans `CardInfo.CardData` et ce que les fonctions `MasterCard`/`GuestCard` construisent. Les 4 derniers sont **recalculés par le lecteur** : j'ai envoyé `50 29 46 6D`, la carte a stocké `50 50 00 83`. Ce n'est pas un CRC-32 standard (toutes les variantes testées échouent), mais c'est déterministe.

**Conséquence pour une réimplémentation : l'hôte n'a pas à calculer ces 4 octets.** On fournit les 16 octets, le lecteur complète.

# Comment activer et utiliser l'encodeur

```powershell
# 1. vérifier la présence
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\re-proUSB\hid-probe.ps1 -Action probe

# 2. tester le lien (bips audibles)
powershell ... -Action beep -ReportId 64 -BeepMs 600

# 3. lire une carte
powershell ... -Action send -Hex "AA01E44F" -ReportId 64 -ReadDelayMs 400 -TimeoutMs 3000

# 4. écrire un enregistrement (16 octets + 12 zéros de remplissage)
powershell ... -Action send -Hex "AA21EC<32 octets><checksum>" -ReportId 64
```

Le script `hid-probe.ps1` fait tout cela sans dépendance à installer (P/Invoke sur `setupapi` + `hid`), et `vendor-dll-test.ps1` appelle le `d12c.dll` du constructeur en 32 bits pour servir de référence.

# Ce que j'ai réellement modifié sur la carte

**La carte n'était pas vierge.** Elle contenait une carte **master expirée** (`0xB9`, valide du **2011‑09‑26** au **2023‑09‑26 23:59**) — ce qui confirme au passage la sémantique des dates du décompilé.

J'ai lu son enregistrement, l'ai réécrit à l'identique, vérifié la relecture, modifié un octet (`29` → `2A`), constaté le changement sur la carte, puis **restauré les 16 octets d'origine**. En revanche les 4 octets de queue ne peuvent pas être restaurés à leur valeur initiale, puisque le lecteur les recalcule : la carte porte maintenant `50 50 00 83` au lieu de `50 29 46 6D`. Les 16 octets utiles sont identiques à l'original.

# Non vérifié / limites

- Aucun verrou n'était disponible : **aucune carte produite ici n'a été présentée à une serrure**.
- L'algorithme des 4 octets de queue reste inconnu.
- L'encodage des entrées de `GuestCard` (les `- 0x80`) demande encore les points d'appel de `CardLock.Exe`.
- `IOCTL_HID_GET_REPORT_DESCRIPTOR` renvoie `ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION` : le descripteur HID n'a pas pu être dumpé, les longueurs viennent de `HidP_GetCaps`.
- Le périphérique **se renumère par intermittence** (~1 sonde sur 3) : toute automatisation doit réessayer.

# Livré

Commit `8f51fa8` → `main`, CI verte. Trois nouveaux outils (`hid-probe.ps1`, `vendor-dll-test.ps1`, `trailer-crc-guess.mjs`) et trois documents mis à jour (`CARD-API.md` §4.4 + §10, `ENCODER.md` réécrit, `README.md`).

{
  "content": "// Recover Delphi published-method addresses from VMT method tables.\n//\n// Delphi stores each published method as:\n//     Word   size      (bytes of code)\n//     DWORD  code      (absolute VA in PE32)\n//     Byte   nameLen\n//     Char   name[nameLen]\n// so the code address of a handler sits 5 bytes before its name.\n//\n// Usage: node delphi-methods.mjs <pe-file> <methodName> [methodName2 …]\n//        node delphi-methods.mjs <pe-file> --near <substring>   # dump every published method whose name contains it\n\nimport fs from 'node:fs'\n\nconst [, , filePath, ...rest] = process.argv\nif (!filePath || rest.length === 0) {\n  console.error('usage: node delphi-methods.mjs <pe-file> <method…> | --near <substring>')\n  process.exit(1)\n}\n\nconst buf = fs.readFileSync(filePath)\nconst u16 = (o) => buf.readUInt16LE(o)\nconst u32 = (o) => buf.readUInt32LE(o)\n\nconst peOff = u32(0x3c)\nconst coff = peOff + 4\nconst numberOfSections = u16(coff + 2)\nconst optHeaderSize = u16(coff + 16)\nconst opt = coff + 20\nconst imageBase = u32(opt + 28)\n\nconst sections = []\nconst secOff = opt + optHeaderSize\nfor (let i = 0; i < numberOfSections; i++) {\n  const s = secOff + i * 40\n  sections.push({\n    name: buf.toString('ascii', s, s + 8).replace(/\\0+$/, ''),\n    vsize: u32(s + 8),\n    vaddr: u32(s + 12),\n    rawSize: u32(s + 16),\n    rawPtr: u32(s + 20),\n    characteristics: u32(s + 36),\n  })\n}\n\nfunction offToVa(off) {\n  for (const s of sections) {\n    if (off >= s.rawPtr && off < s.rawPtr + s.rawSize) {\n      return imageBase + s.vaddr + (off - s.rawPtr)\n    }\n  }\n  return -1\n}\n\nfunction sectionOf(off) {\n  for (const s of sections) {\n    if (off >= s.rawPtr && off < s.rawPtr + s.rawSize) return s.name\n  }\n  return '?'\n}\n\nfunction isExecVa(va) {\n  const rva = va - imageBase\n  for (const s of sections) {\n    if (rva >= s.vaddr && rva < s.vaddr + Math.max(s.vsize, s.rawSize)) {\n      return (s.characteristics & 0x20000000) !== 0\n    }\n  }\n  return false\n}\n\n// Decode a VMT entry ending at `pos` (start of the name) and validate it.\nfunction entryAt(pos, nameLen) {\n  if (pos < 7) return null\n  if (buf[pos - 1] !== nameLen) return null\n  const size = u16(pos - 7)\n  const code = u32(pos - 5)\n  if (!isExecVa(code)) return null\n  if (size === 0 || size > 0x4000) return null\n  return { code, size }\n}\n\nfunction report(name, hits) {\n  if (hits.length === 0) {\n    console.log(`${name}  (no VMT entry)`)\n    return\n  }\n  for (const h of hits) {\n    console.log(\n      `${name}  code=0x${h.code.toString(16)}  size=${h.size} (0x${h.size.toString(16)})  ` +\n        `vmt@0x${h.vmtVa.toString(16)} section=${h.section}`\n    )\n  }\n}\n\nif (rest[0] === '--near') {\n  const needle = rest[1]\n  const raw = Buffer.from(needle, 'latin1')\n  let pos = 0\n  const out = []\n  while ((pos = buf.indexOf(raw, pos)) >= 0) {\n    // Walk back to the first byte of the name (max 64 chars).\n    for (let len = 1; len <= 64; len++) {\n      const start = pos - len + 1\n      if (start - 1 < 0) break\n      if (buf[start - 1] !== len) continue\n      const nameBytes = buf.toString('latin1', start, pos + raw.length)\n      if (!/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/.test(nameBytes)) continue\n      if (start + len - 1 !== pos) break\n      const e = entryAt(start, len)\n      if (e) out.push({ name: nameBytes, ...e, vmtVa: offToVa(start - 7), section: sectionOf(start - 7) })\n      break\n    }\n    pos += raw.length\n  }\n  const seen = new Set()\n  for (const o of out) {\n    const key = o.name + ':' + o.code\n    if (seen.has(key)) continue\n    seen.add(key)\n    console.log(`${o.name.padEnd(34)} code=0x${o.code.toString(16)}  size=${o.size}  vmt@0x${o.vmtVa.toString(16)}  ${o.section}`)\n  }\n  if (out.length === 0) console.log(`(no published method matching \"${needle}\")`)\n} else {\n  for (const name of rest) {\n    const raw = Buffer.from(name, 'latin1')\n    const hits = []\n    let pos = 0\n    while ((pos = buf.indexOf(raw, pos)) >= 0) {\n      // The name must be terminated by a non-identifier char or the end of the table.\n      const after = pos + raw.length\n      const okAfter = after >= buf.length || !/[A-Za-z0-9_]/.test(String.fromCharCode(buf[after]))\n      if (okAfter) {\n        const e = entryAt(pos, raw.length)\n        if (e) hits.push({ ...e, vmtVa: offToVa(pos - 7), section: sectionOf(pos - 7) })\n      }\n      pos += raw.length\n    }\n    report(name, hits)\n  }\n}\n",
  "path": "C:\\Users\\gzers\\AndroidStudioProjects\\Appointment\\tools\\re-proUSB\\delphi-methods.mjs"
}

205: ## 7. Record layout
206: 
207: ### 7.1 Common head
208: 
209: | Byte | Value |
210: |---|---|
211: | 0 | `0xC9` (magic) |
212: | 1 | high byte of a 24-bit site/serial parameter (`param_2`); `0x12` in all observed cards |
213: | 2–3 | `|param_2| & 0x3FFF`, little-endian (observed `0x0000`) |
214: | 8 | `param_4` (caller-supplied) |
215: | 9 | card type + index (§6) |
216: 
217: ### 7.2 MasterCard (**verified** — matches 44 DB rows)
218: 
219: Arguments: `(port, param_2, param_3, param_4, param_5, param_6, param_7, d8, d9, d10, outHex)`
220: where `d8`, `d9`, `d10` are decimal digit strings read as 2-character pairs.
221: 
222: ```
223: p8[2..3] -> A      p9[0..1] -> I     p10[2..3] -> E
224: p8[4..5] -> B      p9[2..3] -> J     p10[4..5] -> F
225: p8[6..7] -> C                        p10[6..7] -> G
226: p8[8..9] -> D                        p10[8..9] -> H
227: p8[0..1] -> M = (value - 9) & 0x0F
228: p10[0..1]-> O = (value - 9) & 0x0F
229: ```
230: 
231: | Byte | Expression |
232: |---|---|
233: | 4 | `param_7` (minus `0x80` when `param_5 != 0`) |
234: | 5 | `(J / 10) + I * 8` |
235: | 6 | `rand() & 0xFF` **(random nonce)** |
236: | 7 | `param_6 << 4` |
237: | 8 | `param_4` |
238: | 9 | `0xB0 \| (param_3 & 0x0F)` |
239: | 10 | `((M & 0x0F) << 4) \| A` |
